data.title: Have metrics disabled by default, or completely removed
data.body:
You need to leave the metrics disabled by default and then at least ask users, first time they activate the editor, whether they would allow it to be enabled.

I for one will not allow spyware to run on my box, hence I disable or remove such applications, but Atom doesn't provide a clue in the application, so if someone haven't seem the FAQ, they don't know.

This is a problem because Atom is then collecting data WITHOUT consent, even if it is in the FAQ and even if the user has downloaded the application.

Besides, I find the whole concept of tracking users with the excuse of collecting useful data ridiculous!

In the entire history of Open Source this has never been needed and users are extremely helpful in sharing information, data, and reports about bugs, how they use the application, and other stuff.

The metrics package in Atom should to be removed from the default install, and then you can leave the package for anyone who want to install it by himself from the installation menu.

data.title: Have metrics disabled by default, or completely removed
data.body:
> I don't believe "anonymously" is correct here: Google Analytics will get my IP number, and they likely save it. IPs are certainly personally identifiable information.

Unless you have a way of systematically / categorically disabling Google (and Yandex and others) Analytics across the Internet, I assure you that some Google Analytics instance already has data based on your IP address.

I just want to reiterate that [Atom's metrics code is completely open source](https://github.com/atom/metrics), so you can see for yourself exactly what data is being collected, and you can always disable it as it's just another package.
[From the Readme](https://github.com/atom/metrics#metrics-package-), this is what is being collected:
> - A unique identifier that is generated by computing the SHA-1 of the machine's MAC address.
- The screen width and height
- The version of Atom being used
- The name of each item opened in a pane such as EditorView, SettingsView, and MarkdownPreviewView
- Exception messages (without paths)
- Commands run (save core commands)
- The amount of time the current window was open for
- The amount of time the current window took to load
- The amount of time the app took to launch
- Deprecations: package name and version of each deprecation

[I've also opened a PR for a new cross-platform "About Atom"](https://github.com/atom/atom/pull/7377) that reiterates the notice about metrics, so it can be more apparent after users dismiss the Welcome Guide.

data.body:
> but why an opt-in would make it useless if it is what all the other companies are doing?

Squirrel does not have an installer GUI, so no checkboxes during installation.  Currently there's no way to toggle settings from URIs (such as the `atom://` handler), so the only way to manually enable metrics if it were disabled by default would be to click on the "Metrics" link on the Welcome page (provided they read it - as is evident further up in this issue not many people bother to read the Welcome page) and then enable it.  This is arguably exactly what people who *want* to disable metrics are doing, but bear in mind those who want to disable metrics usually are a lot more proactive and willing to go through whatever it takes then those who don't care either way.

@andreagrandi The reason opt-in would become fairly useless, if not totally, is that most people wouldn't bother actively enabling it, even if just out of pure laziness.
So those users who do, will be only a tiny proportion of the whole user base, and thus the information you get from it, is merely anecdotal (which could be useful to some extent, granted). In other words: If the devs are after truly representative information about their users, this wouldn't give it to them.

Btw, I'm not sure the cookies law applies here (I'm based in England, I get harassed by that stupidity of a law several times a day).
But I see your point in terms of it being similar and something of a guideline to what European laws expect of product developers.

@FranBar Thanks for the links.
The first page talks about rights and duties regarding the collection of "personal data", referring for details to the [Data Protection Directive](http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:31995L0046&from=en). Now, I have not yet read the whole thing, but maybe you know: Does it include a definition of what *personal* data legally includes? 
And do your [Atom screen width and recent exception messages](https://github.com/atom/metrics/blob/master/README.md) get mentioned?

Everyone, I think this is getting out of hand. It is going around in circles and I don't believe the two camps are in any danger of shifting their positions on this. A few things:

* I, and I believe everyone else here, respect people's choice to disable the metrics package or simply uninstall Atom altogether. Everyone has to make a decision as to how best to protect their own privacy.
* Regarding whether or not things are illegal, I don't believe anyone involved in the discussion is a lawyer in any jurisdiction. I'm certain that GitHub, on the other hand, has a legal department that could advise or has already advised them on what the actual boundaries are. So let's leave the law to the lawyers.
* I would encourage everyone here to refer to the [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/atom/atom/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#code-of-conduct) because I personally feel that the comments here are coming close to the "insulting/derogatory comments" clause under the Code. I want to leave this Issue open to comments but only if it will result in civil and constructive discussion ... not back and forth that will only end in name-calling.

Thanks for listening and being passionate about Atom.

> As I mentioned above, personally I don't care about the data that the metrics package collects, as it's really minor stuff [...]

This must have been gone over before.. but:

https://github.com/atom/metrics#collected-data

> * A unique UUID v4 random identifier is generated according to [RFC4122][RFC4122]
> * The screen width and height
> * The version of Atom being used
> * The name of each view class or atom configuration file opened in a pane, e.g. `EditorView`, `SettingsView`,
  `MarkdownPreviewView`, and `UserKeymap`. No other pane item information is collected.
> * Exception messages (without paths)
> * Commands run (save core commands)
> * The amount of time the current window was open for
> * The amount of time the current window took to load
> * The amount of time the app took to launch
> * The app's release channel (stable, beta, dev)
> * Deprecations: package name and version of each deprecation

---

That is.. extraordinarily minor. Atom has even taken the time to sanitize exception messages (by removing paths). [Microsoft](http://www.infoworld.com/article/2979054/windows-security/windows-7-8-10-now-all-collecting-user-data-for-microsoft.html) collects more. Ubuntu collects more. [Almost](https://www.google.com/analytics/) [every](https://www.intercom.io/) [website](http://get.gaug.es/) collects more.

If it were me.. I'd collect a lot more:
 * Properties of each file opened: `file type`, `size`, `number of lines`, `longest line`, `time to open`, `time to save`
 * A ping to track active usage and how long that looks like
 * Properties of each "ctrl-p" search result: `number of results`, `time to search`, `length of search term`, `position of file in list chosen`
 * Properties of each "find" search result: `number of files in results`, `number of results`, `time to search`, `length of search term`, `number of results visited`.
 * Name and version of each package used (and if its disabled)
 * Number of windows opened
 * How long a window is open for before it is closed (more of active usage)
 * How long a window is idle for (more of active usage)

@batjko Well yes I can definitely see why people would choose to turn it on to help the core developers. Being opt-in is not at odds with because such users can just, opt-in. Basically my view is the ideal of nothing should be phoning home by default. Yes it's great that it's free (for whatever definition of free you mean, gratis or libre), but that still doesn't excuse it collecting usage info by default. As in, it doesn't make it 'perfect' for my 'ideals', and I want to it to be 'perfect', because why not? Or rather, what are the developers really missing out on if it becomes opt-in? If it's just these metrics, then really they should be, in my opinion, making it opt-in because they don't risk 'scaring off' users, and thus potential contributors. (Because you know, how are these metrics *really* useful to atom?)

But I think the only way they can 'justify' keeping it opt-out is if Google is paying them a significant enough amount of money to keep it opt-out (because obviously google knows that making it opt-in will potentially make it useless as you say). Because that way if they make it opt-in, they lose *money*, meaning atom will have less manpower/developers working on it, potentially causing its development to deteriorate. (My personal opinion would be that that doesn't matter since it's free software anyway so the community can keep it going, but I can still understand justifying keeping it opt-out because of money.)

But if you just don't agree with my ideal that nothing should be phoning home by default, then I guess we'll have to agree to disagree and leave it at that.

@mehcode 

> That is.. extraordinarily minor. Atom has even taken the time to sanitize exception messages (by removing paths). Microsoft collects more. Ubuntu collects more. Almost every website collects more.

I don't think this is right. Just because they do "wrong" (in my opinion) things *more*, doesn't excuse another entity from doing "wrong" things less...

Okay, Microsoft collects more, great, but what about those who don't use Windows, then that's a moot point for them. Same with Ubuntu. Yes basically every website engages in 'tracking', but really atom is the only *editor* I've heard that engages in tracking usage stats *by default* (so far). Maybe there are more editors that do this which I haven't heard of, but I certainly don't think it is the norm, is it?

data.title: Have metrics disabled by default, or completely removed
data.body:
@mehcode

> Is there a difference between an editor and a website? Does it matter? This is a strange argument.

Yes. Maybe this is getting blurred with in-browser editors these days, but disregarding that, there is a difference between websites tracking your website visits and editors reporting on what you're doing in the editor.

> It's far different from stealing.. Are you missing any possessions afterwords?

Missing the point, it's not that getting usage stats *is* stealing, it's that it is a 'bad' thing to do (by default), and other people doing bad things does not excuse us from doing bad things as well. So say if they are groups of bad people who actively engage in killing the innocent, it doesn't give us an excuse to kill only a few innocent, saying "oh well, all these other groups do a lot *worse* than us, so it's not *that* bad!". But really the point should be that killing even one innocent person is bad, so it's still not okay to do it. Yes, obviously tracking usage statistics is not the same as murder, I'm not saying it is.

So yes, to agree with this view, you have to agree that phoning home by default is a fundamentally 'bad' thing to do to others. Maybe getting paid a lot of money (by google) justifies this for atom, which I still may not agree with but at least I can understand where they're coming from. But I don't understand keeping it opt-out if that isn't the case, because it doesn't seem like usage statistics alone are all that useful (as in worth it to risk scaring off potential users, and thus contributors). Maybe I'm wrong about that though.

data.title: Have metrics disabled by default, or completely removed
data.body:
You need to leave the metrics disabled by default and then at least ask users, first time they activate the editor, whether they would allow it to be enabled.

I for one will not allow spyware to run on my box, hence I disable or remove such applications, but Atom doesn't provide a clue in the application, so if someone haven't seen the FAQ, they don't know.

This is a problem because Atom is then collecting data WITHOUT consent, even if it is in the FAQ and even if the user has downloaded the application.

Besides, I find the whole concept of tracking users with the excuse of collecting useful data ridiculous!

In the entire history of Open Source this has never been needed and users are extremely helpful in sharing information, data, and reports about bugs, how they use the application, and other stuff.

The metrics package in Atom should to be removed from the default install, and then you can leave the package for anyone who want to install it by himself from the installation menu. Or as suggested, leave it OFF at first.

Another important point is that Atom is NOT simply collecting statistical data! If that where the case there certainly is no need to create a SHA1 of each installation MAC address. That is NOT collecting statistical data, that is specific and individual surveillance, which is unacceptable.
